title: You Can't Tickle Yourself, but a Robot Delayed by 0.2 Seconds Can
hook: Your brain predicts a self-made tickle in advance and cuts it down

open.title: Tickling yourself does nothing, but a robot in the middle changed that
open.line: No matter what you try, you can't tickle yourself. But when scientists put a robot in between, the result changed. What did they change?

summary: A touch you make yourself is predicted by the brain, so it feels weaker. Add a robot and a 0.2 second delay, and it felt just like someone else's tickle.

text: It's hard to stand when someone else tickles you with a feather.
But doing the same thing yourself is far less ticklish.

panels.text: Totally true. It doesn't tickle at all when I do it.

text: The research team tested this with robots.
When the participant moved one robot with the left hand, another robot brushed a soft piece of foam across the right palm.
A touch they made themselves felt less ticklish and less intense than one someone else gave.
The brain, especially the cerebellum, seems to predict the feeling your own movement will cause and cut it down.
In fact, the prediction only had to be thrown off a little.
When the robot moved 0.2 seconds late, the touch could not be told apart from someone else's tickling.
Turning the stroke direction by 90 degrees did the same.
14 of the 16 participants said they did not notice the delay.
